notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1125.tmp1125.opp-lat: The opening paragraphs are run together in the edition under one reference. 'Primasius of Byzacena' is Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum in Byzacena. 'ante 15 aut 16 annus' read as 'annos'. 'constituerat' (end of the devil comparison) read as 'constituerunt'. The phrase 'cesserunt, et ab Ecclesia recesserunt' is a wordplay rendered as 'gave way ... gave way'. 'quam et 'sUe novitru pestes' read as 'quam et istae novitiae pestes'. The scriptural reference 'Joan. v, 50' is a misprint for John 5:30. The sentence 'ut a nullo non damnante ... sciatur an ipsis solis aditus reseratus est inferorum locus' is awkward and possibly corrupt; translated as best the sense allows.

Necrodioctae ('persecutors of the dead') is Facundus's coinage; 'Porcianists' (Porcianistae) is unexplained, and the edition marks it with a note. 'Unless perhaps you wish to tell the truth, and how the heresy... was to come about?' seems corrupt; it is translated as it stands. In the sentence 'My bishop knows whether he condemned anyone', text seems lost before 'he threatens such people'; the gap is marked [...]. The edition marks an omission (....) in the Cyprian quotation. The Cain quotation follows the Septuagint/Old Latin of Gen. 4:7. Scanning errors silently corrected include: 'adsum' read as 'adsunt', 'Inanimam' as 'maximam', 'prece. vestias' as 'preces vestras', 'maxiMus' as 'manibus', 'rt- Iro' as 'retro', '(urem' as 'furem', 'Ici in lectis' as 'Dei in tectis', 'suhi Itis' as 'sub his', 'finitas' as 'unitas'. 'supp'odant' is uncertain; it is read as 'supplodant' ('trip up'). "reserva- / tum" is split across the line break with the previous passage; the sense is "an eternal and endless glorious reward is reserved".

nodes.text: THE LETTER OF FACUNDUS ON THE CATHOLIC FAITH
IN DEFENCE OF THE THREE CHAPTERS.
From volume III of the *Spicilegium* of Dom Luc d'Achery

Some people are troubled and ask what the case of the Three Chapters is, over which the members of Christ are scandalised throughout almost the whole world. They say: what harm can the condemnation that has been made of the Chapters do to the Catholic Church, whether it concerns persons or sayings? Especially, they say, since the condemners themselves profess that they hold the same faith as those who do not condemn, baptise with one creed, and celebrate with one rite both the solemn readings and the order of the sacrifice. Since they press for an account to be given them in short, we must, with the Lord's help, answer them briefly in this way. These very condemners of the Three Chapters cannot deny that their case was settled at the holy council of Chalcedon almost a hundred and twenty years ago. So they must first be made to say whether the Chapters harmed or did not harm the Catholic Church in which they themselves were baptised before the condemnation of the Chapters impiously came about. If they say that they did harm it, they are shown to fasten the mark of error and crime on the Catholic Church. Either it was heretical, which it is wicked to say, since those whom these men condemned as heretics the Church not only did not condemn but even praised, and by the decrees of the synod of Chalcedon declared their sayings orthodox; or at least, wrapped in a cloud of ignorance, it is to be branded by all heresies, since through the course of so many years it did not know, and could not understand, what these men learned fifteen or sixteen years ago, led astray against the apostolic precept by various and strange doctrines, and by obeying the orders of the palace. And so they themselves too are heretics, and baptised by heretics, and not yet reconciled by anyone. For, as they themselves say, those are Catholics who recently condemned or now condemn the Three Chapters and communicate with the condemners; while those are heretics who neither condemned, nor condemn, nor communicate with those who condemn. This being so, either that Church was, as it truly was, and is, and will be, the Catholic Church, which neither condemned nor condemns the Three Chapters, nor communicates with these most wicked condemners and those who communicate with them except after due satisfaction; and then these men are without doubt heretics, who have newly admitted what they did not receive in the Church that regenerated them. Or, if that Church was not the Catholic Church, which it is sacrilege to hear, these men are likewise, all evasions set aside, heretics, because, as has been said, they were baptised by the very Church that never condemned these Chapters. For these reasons, whichever of the two alternatives they answer, they must be convicted as heretics. But if they say, which is true, that these same Chapters did no harm to the Catholic Church through a hundred years and more, as was said above, then far, far more let them understand that they are guilty beyond excuse. Let them consider how much evil they have committed against its decrees by condemning what it did not condemn; let them recognise what they have done, and perceive that they are cut off from it, since, tearing up its decrees as far as lay in them, they have stubbornly joined themselves to the troops of heretics by favouring their wishes. For the condemnation of the Chapters was sought out and extracted by the Acephalous heretics, that is, the Semi-Eutychians; and the writings published against the Church by Vigilius and Pelagius, the prevaricators of Rome, and by Primasius of Byzacena, the foremost teacher of the Acephali, bear witness to it. This being so, how can that other claim now hold for them, when they say that they hold one faith with those who do not condemn? For we confess in our one Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God and of man, the distinctness of two natures in the unity of the person, which the Catholic Church always guards and teaches. But these men, obeying the Acephali, and saying in writing: "We anathematise the impious letter of Ibas which he wrote to Maris the Persian, together with those who defend it and say that it, or part of it, is right," are shown beyond doubt to have anathematised the whole Church, which defended and defends it, and said and says that it is right; since the Church confesses concerning the Incarnation of Christ, in which the mystery of our salvation consists, exactly what that letter contains in every respect. For the words of that same letter, where the soundness of the Catholic confession lies, run thus, after other things: "But the Church says thus: Two natures, one power, one person, which is the one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ." Therefore, if this confession of the two natures of our Lord Jesus Christ in the unity of the person is impious and godless, as these men have said, let them say, as new teachers, what is pious and befitting the right faith of Christians. Surely, then, as the truth, refuting them from their works and writings, forces them to admit, they say either that there is one nature in Christ, as the Eutychians or Acephali say, to whose wishes they gave way and from the Church gave way; or that there is none. How impious and blasphemous this is, and how foreign to Catholic truth, anyone endowed with a sound mind will recognise without hesitation. Next let us examine the claim they make in words, that they baptise with one creed, and whether it is shown to be true of them in fact and in effect. To make this plain, we must first consider and weigh the force and greatness of the truth of the creed itself; for unless that through which one believes comes first, the power and gift of belief, which follows, is in no way granted, as it is written: Unless you believe, you will not understand (Isa. 7:9, according to the Seventy). Our fathers, the Catholic teachers, taught that "symbol" [creed] is to be interpreted as a contribution, or a compact made between man and God. Since, then, we have made a compact with God, and in this way have been baptised in the one name of the Holy Trinity, if anyone undoes one iota or one stroke of the compact he entered into with God, he is without doubt shown to have lost the faith by which he believed God, and God himself in whom he believed. Who it is that have violated this compact we shall soon see, when we have set down the words of the creed itself, not indeed in full order, to avoid length, but by taking samples. The beginning of the creed, then, is this: We believe in one God the Father almighty; and in one Lord Jesus Christ his Son, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried; on the third day he rose from the dead; he ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead, and the rest. Here, surely, the whole question now lies: the judgement of the living and the dead. This was not added to the creed against any heresy at any time, as that article on the equality of the Father and the Son was added at the council of Nicaea against Arius, or that on the omnipotence of the Holy Spirit at Constantinople against Macedonius; and it was never violated by any heresy, except by this one, which has arisen in these last times as if from the combined dregs of all heretics: namely, through the condemnation of the living and the dead, which they put forward in writing, saying among other things: "If anyone defends the impious Theodore and his impious writings, and does not anathematise him and his impious writings, and all who receive or defend him and say that he expounded orthodox [doctrine]; and those who wrote on his behalf and held the same views, or write on behalf of him or of his impious writings, and those who hold or at any time held views like his, let such a one be anathema. If anyone defends the impious writings of Theodoret, and does not anathematise them, and those who held or hold views like his, let such a one be anathema. If anyone defends the impious letter which Ibas is said to have written to Maris the Persian heretic, and does not anathematise it and its defenders, and those who say that it, or part of it, is right, and those who wrote or write on behalf of it, or of the impiety contained in it, and presume to defend it, let such a one be anathema." By this blasphemous sentence they have, as far as lay in them, wrapped in a like anathema both those dead men, whom no one condemned while they were in the body, and whose teaching no one judged heretical, but rather, as can be proved by the clearest documents, the synodal authority of the Fathers declared orthodox, and devout posterity has preserved until now and still preserves; and the very Fathers who praised them and their sayings; and us, who are living. Where then is their wish to be seen and called Christians, and their idle, wordy boasting that they keep the faith of the creed, when with proud and most lamentably rash audacity they have usurped for themselves the judgement which the Father gave to the Son alone, and by such presumption are shown to surpass even the madness of the devil? For he, in the proudest craving of his heart, said: I will be like the Most High (Isa. 14:14). But these men, by forestalling the judgement of God and carrying out with deadly work the condemnation of the dead and the living who do not agree with them, have made themselves, as far as their intention goes, not equal or like to their Lord, as he said still of the future, "I will be," but superior. And the wretches are not ashamed to say, with sacrilegious mouth and shameless insolence, that they hold one faith with the condemners! As if the demons too did not believe and tremble; but they are known to have only the working of error, which these new plagues also exercise, themselves erring and leading others into error. And not only misleading them into error with lying words, but besides, by violent persecutions, dragging and forcing whom they could to agree with them or communicate with them. And the unhappy men do not attend or notice that it does not help them, but rather weighs heavily on them, to profess in words that they know God, but in deeds to deny him. For indeed, if they truly confessed, or others professed on their behalf when they were baptised, that they believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, as the authority of the creed holds, they ought also to have truly believed and patiently waited for the same Son of God and of man, Jesus Christ our Lord, to come from heaven at the appointed time to judge the living and the dead; and not themselves now, with impious and violent cruelty, not only judge both us who are living and the Catholic bishops long dead, but even condemn them with the anathema of what is meant as a perpetual sentence. But perhaps, by their holiness and the power of their wonderful works, as judges of the living and the dead appointed by themselves, or rather by their father the devil, they claim to have raised up these very dead whom they condemned, and so, having heard their case, as the Lord says in the Gospel, As I hear, I judge (John 5:30), they pronounced the sentence of judgement against them. We ask them, then, when they gathered up their ashes brought back to life and raised them, or where they sat to judge. Surely it is in the valley of Jehoshaphat that the Lord will judge all nations, although this also has another meaning. Is Constantinople, then, the valley of Jehoshaphat, where this sacrilege began? Are the other towns and cities the valley of Jehoshaphat, which have subscribed to and accepted the decree put forward for the condemnation of the living and the dead? Let them also say and show where they have placed those they condemned, so that it is known to none who does not condemn but only to the condemners: has the place of the underworld been unbarred to them alone? Let them then tell us, the living, whom they condemned together with those long dead, when they made us die and at once raised us again, as the Catholic Church confesses will happen at, or before, that judgement of the Lord to those whom his coming finds living in the flesh. But if they could not do these and other things, which we believe will come at a time known to God alone, what madness has invaded their hearts, and [what] smoky vanity of theirs, like the dark night of thick and palpable darkness, has blinded their eyes, so that they did not see nor steadfastly hold what they received in the creed when they were baptised? Instead, at their own pleasure, now corrupted by gifts, now enticed by honours and ambitions, now also led astray by the strange, or rather serpentine, cunning of doctrine, and blown upon and puffed up by the wind of pride, they have raised the crests of pride against God, seizing his judgement in advance, founding a new error through the condemnation of the living and the dead, and restoring an old one, since they have become supporters and partners of the Acephali, and have given their right hands to the other heretics, so that they may rescind or condemn the decrees of orthodox bishops whenever and however they please. For it is not, as some ignorant people say, the case of the Three Chapters that is at stake; rather, what is lamented is the condemnation carried out against all the bishops who, from the apostles and the successors of the apostles down to the synod of Chalcedon, at which these same Chapters were judged orthodox, and thereafter down to our own times, persevering in one and the same defence and communion, departed this life as Catholics. This we could show more fully here, by the clearest documents and the truthful arguments of the fathers' traditions, if the restraint of brevity allowed. When these things have been carefully considered and weighed, let everyone judge who fears the judgement of God, who believes and confesses that the Son of God will come at the fitting time, in the form of a servant which he took up for us, as a manifest judge, whom by believing he has learned came hidden in the fullness of time: let him judge whether such men as these, who prove prouder and more outstanding in audacity than the devil, and worse even than the Antichrist, are to be counted even by the name of Christian, and not rather to be called ministers of the Antichrist and to be shunned in every way. This being so, how can it now hold for them that they believe, as they say, in God the Father and in his Son, which comes first in the creed, when what follows there, said specifically of one and the same Christ, who will come to judge the living and the dead, does not hold for them? For these men, as was said and shown above, have hurled the darts of their condemnation both at the long dead and at us, the living. But with these things set out first, let us look at something further. If they say that the dead whom they condemned taught wrongly and wrote books in a heretical sense, we ask them whether, while they lived, they were admonished according to the custom of Catholic observance and discipline to think soundly and rightly, stubbornly resisted, and, convicted of their error, or summoned to some council, as Arius at Nicaea, Macedonius at Constantinople, Nestorius at the first [council of] Ephesus, Eutyches and Dioscorus at Chalcedon, were condemned or not. If they say that this was done, we shall at once demand that the synodal acts be brought forward, as those of these men are produced, in which it may be shown where their error was condemned and where sentence was pronounced against them. If they show this, we ask again how [these acts] lay hidden from the whole Catholic Church through a series of a hundred years and more, when even human laws remove human disputes after thirty years, and our Lord Jesus Christ gave his apostles the power of binding and loosing, as a divine law, only for the things that are on earth. Or where, do we suppose, were these same acts hidden, so that they could recently have come to the knowledge only of the condemners, and not also of those who do not condemn? But if, as is more true and certain, they cannot produce any such proceedings from of old, because in truth they have nothing to produce, we on the contrary produce the synodal letters of the council of Antioch in defence of Theodore and of his sayings, who was condemned by these men, who are now branded with the new name and charge of a heresy, that is, Necrodioctae or Porcianists. Next we point to the acts of the holy synod assembled at Chalcedon, whose authority no one but a heretic contradicts. There not only were the praises of the blessed Theodore received and read out and proclaimed with wonderful glory, but the letter of the venerable Ibas also, which these men have condemned as impious, is shown to have been declared orthodox there and praised. It was also acclaimed in the same synod that the teaching of Theodoret had long been, and from the beginning, in harmony with the orthodox faith, and both of them, that is, Theodoret and Ibas, were judged worthy of the episcopate and were appointed to govern, as before, the churches entrusted to them. Having first shown these things, we put this question to these condemners of the Chapters and of ourselves, and to those in communion with them: what do they think of this same great council of Chalcedon? Do they call it Catholic or not? If they say, 'It is Catholic,' we answer: 'Then you are beyond doubt heretics. For what those Fathers presiding there praised, and whom they praised, and declared to agree with the Catholic faith, you have condemned as heretical and impious. From this it follows, whether you will or not, as the consequence of reason demands, that those whom they condemned as heretics, that is, Nestorius, Eutyches and Dioscorus, you declare and proclaim orthodox, if not in words, perhaps out of fear of men, then certainly in deeds: by unbridled persecutions, by the expulsion of Catholic bishops and the substitution of heretics, and by condemnations issued in writing against Catholics.' Finally, in one and the same synod of Chalcedon, among the other things defined, this matter too stands settled, namely the approval and the condemnation of three. For see, on one side of that council stand, as it were, Theodore, though already dead, yet living in the synodal letters containing his praises, which were left there and approved; and Theodoret and Ibas, praised and declared orthodox. And on the other side likewise stands Nestorius, condemned indeed at the first [council of] Ephesus, but bound again at Chalcedon with the chain of condemnation; and Eutyches and Dioscorus, likewise condemned there as heretics. What do you say? Is it not so? However thick the callus of hardness with which your brow is covered by your usual lies, will you be able to deny that it is so? And if, in your double confusion, you wish to deny it, see, here are the acts of the council of Chalcedon; see, the six hundred and thirty bishops assembled there stand by. They cry out, indeed, through [the acts] and say: 'We received and approved the praises of Theodore, who died in the peace and communion of the Catholic Church, when they were read out to our assembly. We declared the venerable Theodoret and Ibas orthodox, and we know truly that they subscribed with us to the definition of the Catholic faith. The letter which the venerable Ibas wrote to Maris the Persian, read out before us, we judged to be orthodox, and we confirmed our judgement by subscribing in concord. Nestorius, condemned before, we struck down with a repeated condemnation, together with Eutyches and Dioscorus, the Holy Spirit presiding over us. Whoever strives to violate our judgement is a heretic; whoever attempts to overturn our decrees in any point is a stranger to the Catholic faith, a stranger to the Christian name. For whoever condemns those whom we praised, declaring them Catholic, on the contrary praises those whom we condemned as heretics; and so whoever does not assent to what we have rightly defined, whoever proudly rebels against what was determined in lawful and Catholic order, is a heretic.' Hearing this, what, we ask, will you say to so many illustrious bishops, or to the universal Catholic Church spread through the whole world, which has always devoutly kept their statutes and keeps them to this day in its remnants, spread everywhere? Unless perhaps you wish to tell the truth, and [say] how the heresy of the Necrodioctae or Porcianists was to come about? But if they say, 'The council of Chalcedon is heretical,' there is no further need to contend afresh against them, except that they should be regarded by all who are truly Catholic like the one who, when asked by the Lord in the Gospel what his name was, answered: 'Legion, for we are many' (Mark 5:9). For in truth whoever presumes or attempts to contradict the authority of the holy and great synod of Chalcedon in any point is an Arian, a Macedonian, a Nestorian, a Eutychian and an Acephalus, or whatever can be derived from the various shoots of heretical impiety and fitted to them. Against both these plagues the attention of that synod kept watch, so as to strike past heretics with a repeated condemnation, to anathematise present ones, and, by the prophetic Spirit of God, to bind future ones, with their followers and partakers in any way, in the chains of condemnation. Now as to their saying that they celebrate the solemn readings and the order of the sacrifice with the same rite, we could answer briefly that, for those cut off from Catholic unity, as we have shown, an invocation of the divine name made with feigned words profits nothing, nor does a celebration usurped and drawn away from the Church. For the devil too, tempting the Lord, cited testimonies of the Scriptures, but [testimonies] by which he would be destroyed, not by which he would be strengthened; and the holy Scriptures themselves consist not in reading but in understanding; and various heretics, once cut off, have kept perniciously and lethally what they had received well and wholesomely in the Catholic [Church]. We could also say about the sacrifice what the Lord said to Cain at the beginning of the world: 'If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.' And also what the same Lord says through the prophet to priests who transgress and violate God's covenant: 'When you multiply your prayers, I will turn my face away from you. And when you offer me sacrifice, I will not receive it from your hands, nor will I be appeased toward you, for your assemblies are wicked' (Isa. 1:13, 15); and many similar things which it would take long to recount. But we have judged it fitting also to bring forward one or two testimonies of the most glorious martyr and bishop Cyprian, written against such men in a similar case, because whoever is understanding in heart, having considered and examined them carefully with the eyes of the heart, will see whether he ought any longer to seek the sacrifices of the new heretics. For in his letter to Magnus, written on behalf of saint Cornelius, likewise martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, whom the heretic Novatian had driven out and put himself in his place, as has now also been done by the new heretics, he says after other things: "But if the flock is one, how can one be counted in the flock who is not in the number of the flock? Or how can he be held a shepherd who, while the true shepherd remains and presides in the Church of the Lord by ordained succession, himself succeeds no one and begins from himself, and so becomes an alien and profane, an enemy of the Lord's peace and of divine unity, not dwelling in the house of God, that is, in the Church of God, in which only those of one mind and heart dwell? Finally, how inseparable is the sacrament of unity, and how hopeless are those, and what very great ruin they bring on themselves from the wrath of God, who make a schism and, abandoning their bishop, set up another, a false bishop, for themselves.... But if anyone objects, saying that Novatian holds the same law which the Catholic Church holds, baptises with the same creed as we, knows the same God the Father, the same Son, Christ, the same Holy Spirit, let whoever thinks this should be objected know that this cannot help such men. For Korah, Dathan and Abiram also knew the same God as the priest Aaron and Moses; living under the same law and religion, they called upon the one true God, who was to be worshipped and called upon. Yet because, overstepping the ministry of their place, they claimed for themselves the licence to sacrifice against the priest Aaron, who had received the lawful priesthood by God's favour and ordination, they were struck by God and at once paid the penalty for their unlawful attempts; nor could sacrifices offered irreligiously and unlawfully against the right of divine ordinance be valid and profitable. Therefore those who champion Novatian or others of this kind contend in vain. And so that it might be better understood what the divine judgement is against such audacity, we find that in such a crime not only the leaders and authors but also the partakers are destined for punishment, unless they separate themselves from the communion of the wicked, for the Lord commands through Moses, saying: 'Separate yourselves from the tents of these most hardened men, and do not touch anything that is theirs, lest you perish together in their sin' (Num. 16:26). And what the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled, so that whoever had not separated himself from Korah, Dathan and Abiram at once paid the penalty for impious communion. By this example it is shown and proved that all are liable to both guilt and punishment who with irreligious rashness join themselves to schismatics against the prelates and priests of God; as the Holy Spirit also testifies through the prophet Hosea, saying: 'Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled' (Hos. 9:4), teaching, that is, and showing that all without exception who have been defiled by their sin are joined with the authors in punishment." What can be said more evident than this testimony? What clearer? What truer? For see, he teaches that all without exception, however many have been polluted by communion with the wicked, are bound by equal guilt and equal punishment. What then of the fact that some say, as if excusing themselves: 'My bishop knows whether he condemned anyone'? [...] he threatens such people, saying: 'But you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you put your portion with adulterers' (Ps. 49:17-18). And below, the apostle Paul (Rom. 1:32) makes clear and proves that not only those who do evil are worthy of death and come to punishment, but also those who consent to those doing such things: those who mix with the wicked, with sinners and with the unrepentant in unlawful communion are polluted by contact with the guilty, and as they are joined in guilt, so they are not separated in punishment either. But these men say: 'But we do not consent to the condemnation of the dead.' O intolerable evil! O unheard-of disgrace! They say they do not consent, in words as it were, to the condemnation, and they consent in deeds, which is worse, to an execrable communion; whereas a heavier punishment awaits those who do not ignore the truth and yet communicate with the enemies of the truth. For if those with whom you communicate made a heresy, as we have shown, by condemning the living and the dead; if they went over to the heretics by doing what the Acephali wanted, then both have certainly remained heretics through what they committed. How then will those who communicate with heretics be denied to be held by the charge of heresy? Or with what face do they think they communicate with the Catholic [Church]? Or because, propped up by the palace's support, they have seized churches made by hands after driving out the Catholics, do you therefore think that the Catholic faith and Christian peace lie in walls? If you think so, hear what saint Hilary too, bishop, confessor and outstanding teacher, writes on this matter to certain bishops in the time of the emperor Constantius, when the Arians, under the name of peace and of the king, had seized almost all the local churches of the whole world, as the Eutychians or Acephali now have. He says, after other things: "I ask you, bishops, you who believe yourselves to be such, what support did the apostles use for preaching the Gospel? Helped by what powers did they preach Christ and bring almost all the nations over from idols to the Lord? Did they take on themselves any dignity from the palace?" And below he says: "One thing I warn you: beware of Antichrist. For a love of walls has wrongly seized you; wrongly do you venerate the Church of God in roofs and buildings; wrongly do you thrust the name of peace beneath these. Is it doubtful that Antichrist will sit in these? Mountains and woods and lakes and prisons and chasms are safer to me. For in these the prophets abode, and prophesied by the Spirit of God." Let these testimonies, brought forward for brevity, suffice for now, since if we wished to heap up more or to reason further, we might perhaps burden the memory of readers. Now we must also briefly mention what they object from the works of blessed Augustine written against the Donatists, saying: 'Saint Augustine said: Peace is good, have peace; unity is good, love unity, let unity not be split.' But they in no way perceive how much these and similar testimonies of the outstanding teacher trip them up and establish us. For if these men, who rather object these things against themselves, did not wish to split unity, if they did not wish to wage war on the Catholic Church, by which peace would be violated, then what they found in it they ought certainly to have preserved and manfully guarded, as was shown above. And what they did not receive from it, or it did not receive, they ought to have fled and shunned as truly harmful and lethal. For peace is to be had, according to the apostolic teaching, with all men, if it can be, yet not to be held with all. For it is one thing to have something, quite another to hold it. Not only with schismatics and heretics, then, but even with carnal Jews and pagans peace is to be had. But that peace, surely, by which we desire and long to win them for God and to join them to Catholic truth and unity; for which reason we also pray for them, according to God's command, that they may be converted; not to be held in such a way that we go out to them and become ourselves what they are. Finally, what blessed Augustine said and urged on the Donatists, to have peace, to love unity, he said quite excellently and wholesomely: for he desired that they, as we desire these men, should condemn their error and return to the Catholic [Church], as he teaches most clearly in many works written against their schism; not that he himself, or any of the orthodox, should abandon the Catholic [Church], God forbid, and mix in the sacrilegious communion of their error. This we too say to these men in great peace: Condemn the error you have introduced, remove the evil of condemnation you have brought in, by which you have both become heretics and shown yourselves supporters of heretics; and, having peace with us and holding it as before, you will have confounded all heretics and restored yourselves to Catholic unity. Whoever you are, then, who read this, do not look for eloquence, but consider carefully the substance and weight of the truth. And if you are not polluted by the communion of transgressors, pray God that you may persevere. But if you have fallen, whether through ignorance or under force, hasten to repair [your fall] by running back to Catholic truth and taking up its communion again; for pardon is promised to all who repent. Let no one be broken by despair. Let no one be further entangled by serpentine deceptions: for as everlasting punishment with the devil is prepared for transgressors and those who remain with an impenitent heart, so by the Lord God, for those who keep his covenant, guard the foundations of the Catholic faith and avoid profane novelties, an eternal and endless glorious reward is reserved.
